analysis.one_liner: Fines oil companies up to $100 million for fuel price increases that outrun their costs.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by a single House member with no cosponsors, referred to committee, and never received a vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Secretary of Energy to write rules within three months barring "unreasonable" price increases on crude oil, residual fuel oil, and refined petroleum products sold in the U.S. [S3]. An unreasonable increase was defined as any price rise that exceeds the company's concurrent increases in production or operating costs directly related to the product [S3]. Violators could face civil penalties of up to $100 million per unreasonable increase, and the Energy Information Administration would review at least annually whether any company had violated the rules [S3]. It was referred to the House Commerce Committee and its Energy and Power Subcommittee, where it died without any hearing, markup, or vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers of gasoline, home heating oil, and other petroleum products, who would gain a new federal check on fuel prices that rise faster than the oil company's own costs. A driver or homeowner paying more at the pump or for heating oil during a price spike would, in principle, get relief if the Energy Department found the increase unreasonable [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the Secretary of Energy to issue regulations prohibiting unreasonable price increases on crude oil, residual fuel oil, and refined petroleum products sold in the United States, with civil penalties of up to $100 million per violation.

An "unreasonable price increase" is defined as any increase exceeding the company's concurrent rises in production or operating costs directly related to the product, so companies could not pass through price hikes beyond their own cost growth.

The Energy Information Administration must determine at least annually whether any energy-producing company has implemented an unreasonable price increase, creating an ongoing enforcement check rather than a one-time review.
The bill gave the Energy Secretary only three months after enactment to issue the regulations, so relief could have arrived quickly for consumers facing price spikes.

analysis.who_pays: Energy-producing companies — crude oil producers, refiners, and sellers of refined petroleum products — would face new federal price regulation and civil fines of up to $100 million per unreasonable increase, plus compliance costs from annual EIA reviews. If the rules deterred price increases that reflected genuine market scarcity, some of the cost could show up as shortages or longer lines instead of higher prices [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill's standard is vague and potentially hard to enforce: it would penalize any price increase that exceeds "concurrent" increases in the company's production or operation costs directly related to the product, but fuel prices are set by crude oil markets and refinery supply constraints that a single company may not control, so honest compliance could be impossible to prove or disprove.

Penalizing price increases above cost could discourage companies from selling fuel during genuine shortages — a company that raises prices in response to scarce supply to ration demand would risk a $100 million fine, which could worsen shortages and lead to rationing or empty pumps.

Enforcement is backward-looking: the Energy Information Administration would determine violations at least annually, meaning consumers would not get relief during the price spike itself, only the possibility of a fine after the fact.

The bill assigns enforcement to the Energy Department and EIA, agencies without established price-regulation and penalty machinery for this task, so the rules would face years of implementation and likely legal challenges before having any practical effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea addresses a real grievance — fuel prices that spike faster than costs — but the bill is crudely designed. Its "unreasonable increase" standard ignores market-wide causes of price swings like crude supply and refinery capacity, and the annual review means consumers get no relief when prices actually spike. A fair reading is that it offered a symbolic response to gas price frustration more than a workable price-regulation mechanism, which may be part of why it drew no cosponsors.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Commerce Committee and its Energy and Power Subcommittee until the Congress ended, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. James Traficant (D-OH) introduced the Fuel Pricing Fairness Act of 2000 on March 9, 2000, the same day it was referred to the House Committee on Commerce.
On May 24, 2000, the bill was referred to the Commerce Committee's Subcommittee on Energy and Power, which took no further action on it.
Traficant delivered introductory remarks on the measure on June 12, 2000, but no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.
The bill had no cosponsors, and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, without the bill advancing out of committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil producers, refiners, and gasoline marketers are better off because the bill died: no federal penalty regime for price increases they judged 'unreasonable' ever took effect, and fuel prices remained governed by market forces.

for.name: Rep. James Traficant, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, delivered introductory remarks on it, and had no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Commerce (106th Congress)
against.role: Committee of referral for the bill
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Energy and Power Subcommittee on May 24, 2000, and never held a hearing, marked it up, or reported it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a vote or a roll call, and its sole sponsor was a Democrat with no cosponsors from either party, so no party split is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have subjected crude oil, residual fuel oil, and refined petroleum product prices to a federal prohibition on increases exceeding the company's own cost growth, with civil fines up to $100 million per violation. Its death left oil companies free to price fuel at market rates without a federal cost-justification check. [S3]

Retailers and distributors would have faced the same federal review of their pricing decisions, though as a lower-cost market tier they would likely have felt the rules less directly than producers. The bill's defeat left their pricing untouched. [S3]
